content: Patients presenting with discharging ulcers or burns may sometimes require referral by peripheral healthcare workers to confirm uncertain diagnoses. Such referrals are considered urgent, as initiating leprosy treatment promptly is critical to halting disease transmission and preventing complications. In regions where leprosy is less common, the ability of general health workers to suspect and refer cases to specialized units is a vital skill. Diagnosis confirmation should occur at specialized referral centers equipped with the necessary medications for treatment initiation and the capacity for initial follow-up care. Once treatment is initiated, ongoing care can be delegated to community-based peripheral health facilities, provided these facilities receive adequate training from referral centers on managing potential side effects and identifying reactions in a timely manner. Referral centers should handle complex leprosy complications, while rehabilitative surgical services are typically centralized. In some cases, mobile units may provide referral services. Community-based organizations (CBOs), non-governmental organizations (NGOs), and private institutions often deliver leprosy services closer to affected communities. Networking with these organizations, along with referral centers, medical colleges, and dermatologists, is crucial to providing comprehensive, patient-centered care. Collaboration with other sectors, both public and private, as well as with community organizations and self-help groups for individuals affected by leprosy, is essential to improving access to care and maintaining high-quality services. In countries with a high burden of leprosy, national coalitions of stakeholders can help raise funds, increase awareness, and create demand for quality services. However, in some countries, leprosy programs are still managed through vertical structures, either independently or integrated with tuberculosis (TB) or neglected tropical disease (NTD) programs. In areas with limited resources, at least one central unit should be designated to oversee leprosy control, ensuring the capacity to detect, treat, and report cases accurately. National authorities bear the ultimate responsibility for leprosy control and elimination, with partners playing a supportive role in sustaining political commitment. Following the declaration of leprosy elimination, many countries have experienced reduced resources for leprosy activities, contributing to delayed detection and an increase in disability rates at diagnosis. This delay is partly due to a loss of expertise and insufficient involvement of the private sector, which is particularly important in regions like Asia and Africa. The Bangkok Declaration of 2013, signed by health ministers from high-burden countries, has helped renew momentum in leprosy elimination efforts. However, as leprosy becomes rarer and other health priorities emerge, addressing the disease has become increasingly challenging. Expanding partnerships beyond traditional leprosy-focused organizations to include those working in disability and social development may offer new opportunities. Improved coordination among traditional leprosy partners, such as NGOs and research institutions, is also necessary to avoid duplication of efforts and enhance service delivery. Adequate funding and political will, along with partnerships and better coordination in key areas like research, are foundational to achieving the goals outlined in the Global Leprosy Strategy. Ministries of Health should lead national leprosy responses, employing regulatory approaches such as mandatory disease notification while ensuring patient privacy and harmonized drug policies. Sustaining interventions for detection, care, and prevention requires high-level political commitment, sound planning, and sufficient financial and human resources. Universal Health Coverage (UHC) presents an opportunity to advance leprosy control by ensuring access to quality health services for all, particularly for vulnerable and marginalized populations. In countries with a high leprosy burden, integrating leprosy services into broader NTD programs can help retain expertise and improve service inclusion at all levels of care. In low-burden settings, partnerships with other public health programs can strengthen the leprosy network, ensuring efficient case detection and management. Research remains critical to addressing gaps in understanding leprosy transmission, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. Despite the discovery of the causative agent in 1873, much about the disease's pathogenesis and immunological mechanisms remains unknown. Coordination among research institutions and alignment with national programs are essential to avoid duplication and mobilize resources effectively. Finally, partnerships with private and non-profit organizations can enhance access to lifelong protective tools, reconstructive surgery, and social care for individuals affected by leprosy. National coalitions should be established to coordinate efforts, raise awareness, and advocate for increased resources for leprosy control. Ministries of Health must lead these efforts, ensuring effective donor coordination and involving all partners in planning and evaluation processes.
